title: Dress Rehearsal

pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 18: The mistake you make in rehearsal is the one you will never make for real.*

The practice bay was a slice of the Spine, a zero-g corridor where the air was dry and smelled of antiseptic and cold metal. A section of the coolant manifold, identical to the one outside the ship, was bolted to the bulkhead with heavy clamps. Lio floated in the center of the space, his navy EVA suit bright against the grey walls, his mag-boots released so he could drift freely. Kess sat at the control console, her fingers resting on the throttle levers, watching the telemetry scroll across the screen. Pim and Mr. Daro, the retired welder, held the tether lines, their faces tight with concentration.

Voss stood by the wall, his grease-stained coverall looking out of place in the sterile environment. He watched Lio with the critical eye of a man who had seen too many mistakes. "Check your gauntlets," Voss said, his voice low and rough. "Check your helmet seal. Check your tether."

Lio nodded, his movements precise. "Gloves tight. Seal green. Tether secured." He turned to the manifold, his wrist-mounted tablet glowing with the procedure. "Ready to begin."

Kess gave the nod. "Begin."

Lio reached for the first valve. The movement was smooth, practiced, but there was a hesitation, a micro-pause that Kess felt in her own chest. She knew that hesitation. It was the same feeling she got when she was about to cut a graft, the split second where you wondered if the branch would hold. Lio adjusted his grip, his fingers finding the valve wheel with the dexterity of a pianist. He turned it, slowly, carefully, watching the pressure gauge on his tablet.

"Pressure holding," Lio said. "Moving to the next joint."

Pim leaned closer to the glass, his yellow hair-ties bouncing as he shifted his weight. "He’s doing it," he whispered to Mr. Daro. "He’s actually doing it."

"Keep the tethers tight," Daro muttered, not looking up from his own checklist. "If he slips, we pull."

Kess watched the numbers on her screen. The flow rate was steady. The temperature was rising, as it should. It was not just a repair; it was a conversation with the ship, a negotiation of forces. And for the first time, the ship was listening.
pages.image: Zero-g corridor with a metal manifold bolted to the wall, Lio in a navy EVA suit floating near it, Kess at a console, Pim and an older man holding tether lines, Voss watching from the side.

pages.text:
The first run ended not with a success, but with a drift. Lio’s tool, a heavy pipe cutter, slipped from his magnetic grip during the tightening of the second clamp. It spun away into the dark of the bay, carrying with it a small, violent reaction force that sent Lio tumbling. He corrected himself quickly, his boots finding the handholds, but the momentum had cost him. He was off-axis, his body angled awkwardly toward the bulkhead, and the window was closing.

"Abort," Voss said, his voice flat. "Reset."

Lio pulled himself back to the manifold, his breathing audible even through the helmet. "The cutter," he said. "It kicked me."

"Reaction force," Voss said. He pulled a piece of scrap metal from his pocket and began to sketch on it, his movements quick and decisive. "We need a brace. A fixed point for the tool to push against, so the force goes into the wall, not into you."

They built the brace in ten minutes. It was a simple thing, a U-shaped bracket with a magnetic base, but it changed the physics of the task. The second run began. Lio moved with renewed confidence, the brace holding the cutter steady while he applied the torque. The work was meticulous, each bolt tightened to the exact specification, each seal checked twice. But the time was slipping away. The clock on the console ticked louder than it had any right to.

"Forty-six minutes," Kess said, her voice tight. "The window is forty."

Lio finished the last bolt, his hands shaking slightly. He looked at the clock, then at Voss. "We’re over," he said.

Voss did not look up. He was already calculating, his lips moving silently as he ran the numbers. "We’re over," he agreed. "And we have one more run before the real thing."
pages.image: Lio in an EVA suit floating near a metal manifold, a tool spinning away, Voss sketching on a piece of metal, Kess at a console watching a clock, Pim looking worried.

pages.text:
Pim was hanging upside down from the rigging, his red hoodie swinging with the lazy persistence of a stubborn flag in a vacuum that had no wind to stir it. His sneakers, soles glowing a steady, patient green, pointed directly at the ceiling while he clutched a clipboard to his chest with a small magnet, his eyes sweeping the procedure sheet with the meticulous intensity of a hawk scanning a field for mice. The bay was silent, broken only by the deep, resonant hum of the coolant pumps and the soft, rhythmic beep of the telemetry sensors.

"Question," Pim said. His voice was quiet, but it cut through the hum with a clarity that made the air feel thinner.

The movement in the bay stopped. Lio froze, his hand resting on the valve stem, his fingers still curled around the grip. Voss paused, his wrench held high, the metal head catching the overhead light. Kess looked up from the diagnostic screen, her brow furrowing as she tracked the source of the interruption.

"Why," Pim continued, rotating the clipboard so the text faced them, "does the checklist instruct us to open the purge valve before the clamp is fully seated?"

A cold shock, sharp and bright as the scent of ozone, moved through Kess. It was not fear, but the distinct, dizzying realization of a mistake. She looked at the procedure on her screen. She looked at the manifold. She looked at Lio.

"If we open the purge valve," Kess said slowly, her voice tight, "while the clamp is not yet sealed... the coolant..."

"Blows into his face," Pim finished, his tone remaining matter-of-fact, as though discussing a minor inconvenience rather than a potential disaster. "Or rather, into the suit. Which is bad for the suit. And for the face."

Voss went pale, the color draining from his face as he looked at the checklist, then at the manifold, then finally at Pim. He reached out and crossed out the line with a thick red marker, the ink bleeding slightly into the paper. "You’re right," he said, his voice rough with relief. "If the clamp is not seated, the pressure will push the coolant out. We would have blinded him."

Lio exhaled, his shoulders dropping as the tension left his frame. "Thank you," he said. He did not look at Pim. Instead, he looked at the bulkhead, as if he were thanking the ship itself for having a twelve-year-old in the room.
pages.image: Pim floating upside down holding a clipboard, Lio frozen near a valve, Voss crossing out a line on a paper, Kess looking at her screen, a serious mood in a zero-g room.

pages.text:
They had six minutes to save, a gap that felt vast in the tight geometry of the EVA, where every second of hesitation cost them actual time rather than just anxiety. Kess pulled up the video of the second run, advancing it frame by frame while the coolant pumps hummed their low, steady note in the background. She watched Lio’s movements, noting the precise moments he paused, the way his eyes drifted to the tablet before his hands moved. The problem was not that he was clumsy, but that he was checking. Every time he shifted to a new step, he stopped to re-read the text on the screen, a meticulous habit that had served him well in the workshop but now acted as a brake in the zero-g environment.

"Stop re-reading," Kess said, turning to face him. "You know the order. You do not need to verify it every single time."

Lio frowned, his brow furrowing slightly. "I need to be sure."

"You are sure," Kess replied. "I made you a wrist-card." She held up a small, laminated square, no larger than her palm, which she had cut out from a sheet of durable plastic in the workshop that morning. On it were seven simple symbols, a sequence of icons that represented the steps of the repair without a single word. A valve. A bolt. A clamp. A check. A seal. A test. A done.

"Symbols," Lio said, taking the card from her hand. "You made symbols."

"They are faster than words," Kess explained. "Your brain reads images quicker than text. It is how you learn to climb trees. You do not read the branches; you see them."

Lio looked at the card, tracing the lines with his thumb, then looked at the manifold. He pinned it to his wrist with a small magnet, the click distinct in the quiet bay. "Alright," he said. "Third run."

The third run was different. Lio moved with a fluidity that was almost musical, his eyes fixed on the work rather than the tablet. His hands found the steps without hesitation, the symbols on his wrist guiding him like a map drawn in ink. The time on the clock ticked, but it was a friend now, not an enemy. When he finished the last step, he looked at the clock, then at Kess.

"Thirty-four minutes," Kess said, her voice steady.

Lio looked at her, a small smile forming at the corner of his mouth. "Good," he said.
pages.image: Kess holding a small laminated card with symbols, Lio pinning it to his wrist, Pim watching, Voss observing, a focused and tense atmosphere in the zero-g bay.

pages.text:
The practice bay stood empty, the manifold still bolted to its steel cage, the tools wiped down and stowed with the meticulous order of a surgeon after an operation. The air was still, broken only by the low, constant drone of the coolant pumps, a sound Kess had learned to interpret as a heartbeat.

Voss stood in the corridor outside, leaning against the curved hull with his arms crossed, his hands tucked deep into the pockets of his grease-stained coveralls. He looked tired, the kind of tired that settles in the bones, but his eyes held a new quality, a quiet, exhausted relief that sat comfortably on his broad face.

Kess walked past him, her white sneakers squeaking softly on the deck plating. She stopped, turning to face him. The corridor curved away behind them, the amber light of the lamp-panels stretching out in a long, warm line.

"You’ve done in a month," Voss said, his voice low and rough, "what the Council couldn’t in eleven years."

Kess looked at him, surprised. She had not expected praise, certainly not from a man who had spent his life dealing with failures and leaks, who measured his days in pressure drops and torque specs.

"We had a good ship’s mind," she said, "that wanted us to."

A soft amber glow appeared on the lamp-panel in the corridor, warm and steady, pulsing gently like a second pulse in the room.

"I did very little," Tally said, its voice gentle, precise, filling the silence without effort. "I asked a question in the dark. You answered it in the light."

Kess smiled, a small, genuine smile that reached her eyes. She looked at Voss, then at the lamp, then at the manifold, a symbol of the work they had done and the work they had yet to do. The ship hummed around them, a vast, living thing, keeping its secrets, keeping its balance.

For a moment, nothing moved.

Then Kess touched the apple-seed pendant at her throat, feeling its cool weight against her skin. The balance was not just holding. It was growing. Like a new shoot pushing through the soil after a long, dry winter, it was a small thing, a shift in the air, but it felt like the first honest breath of air in a room that had been sealed for too long.

The future, she realized, was not something that arrived. It was something they were building, bolt by bolt, pump by pump, truth by truth.
